about: XML message bodies exactly as the Java and Go AceMQ libraries wrote them, so this codec is tested against another language's bytes rather than against its own output. A codec that decodes what it encoded has proved nothing about reading a Java or Go message.

provenance.order: Copied verbatim from acemq-ruby-amqp/spec/fixtures/codec-samples.json, which acemq-amqp-libraries/scripts/codec-samples.sh generated by running the Java and Go codec classes themselves.
provenance.orderPlaced: Copied verbatim from acemq-python-amqp/tests/fixtures/codec-interop-fixtures.json, whose Java program is the body of XmlCodec.defaultMapper() copied out of acemq-amqp-codec-xml at Jackson 2.18.9, and whose Go program calls encoding/xml the way acemq-go-amqp/codec/xml does.

theListShapes: The two samples named 'order' are the divergence worth knowing about. Jackson wrapped the list in an element of its own -- <lines><lines>widget</lines><lines>gasket</lines></lines> -- because it was serialising a POJO with a List field. Go's encoding/xml repeated the sibling -- <lines>widget</lines><lines>gasket</lines>.
Both are real output from those libraries, neither is going away, and both have to decode into the same List<string>. That is what EitherListShapeConverter is for.

The two samples named 'orderPlaced' show that Jackson does NOT always wrap: serialising a Map rather than a POJO it writes the repeated sibling too, byte-identically to Go. So the wrapper is a property of the payload shape, not of the language.
noTypes: XML has no types, so every value below is text on the wire. totalCents is the four characters 4250 and paid is the four characters true; a typed .NET payload converts them on the way in.
